Preparing SKA Software on French Supercomputers: The DDF Pipeline

How the DDF Pipeline is being hardened into production-ready FR SRCNet software, from a computer-science view: what a run consumes, what it produces, and how it scales.

Research note · November 26, 2026 · 3 min read

One application, one use case

ECLAT, the Extreme Computing Lab for Astronomical Telescopes, is a joint laboratory and a centre of excellence for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence applied to astronomical instrumentation. It brings together sixteen laboratories and teams, including CNRS, Inria, Eviden, the OCA and the Observatoire de Paris.

ASTRA, the ANR–NumPEx project “Alliance for Scalable Techniques in Radio Astronomy”, sits one layer above the software. Led by Marc-Antoine Miville-Deschênes at LPENS, it prepares the technological foundation of the French SKA Regional Centre. The DDF Pipeline is one scientific application inside one ASTRA use case — the Widefield Radio Continuum Surveys case.

The workflow, read as data logistics

The five steps that turn a LOFAR pointing into a science-ready catalogue are, read as a computer scientist, a chain of data volumes moving between sites:

  1. Direction-independent calibration and flagging runs on the LOFAR Long-Term Archive sites — Amsterdam, Jülich and Poznań — where the raw data live. Dysco compression shrinks an 8-hour pointing to roughly 50 GB.
  2. Direction-dependent (DDE) calibration and imaging runs the DDF Pipeline — killMS for calibration, DDFacet for imaging — mostly at the University of Hertfordshire, with smaller volumes at Bologna, Leiden and Hamburg.
  3. Archived products total about 120 GB per 8-hour dataset, held on SURF storage in the Netherlands.
  4. Polarisation and RM-synthesis run pyrmsynth over about 35 GB of Stokes Q and U FITS per 16 deg² field. The polarisation signal is Fourier-transformed along the frequency axis to recover, for each line of sight, the Faraday rotation measure — the magnetic field between the source and the telescope.
  5. Source catalogues list 4 million sources.

The widefield case is where the volumes stop being a sequence and become a rate. The ASTRA project states 250 PB of raw data accumulated from 25,000 hours of observations across 3,168 pointing centres, each observed for 8 to 12 hours, feeding 250 publications over five years — and, for the SKA era it is preparing for, an expected data rate of about 2 TB per observation hour. The DDF Pipeline has processed LoTSS routinely since 2016.

What one run consumes and produces

The profiling in arXiv 2509.03075 reads the pipeline as a resource budget. One representative run starts from 24 MeasurementSet tar-archives: 38.72 GB compressed, 134.4 GB once decompressed. It produces 594 GB in total, of which the 15 images amount to about 17.92 GB — 11 full-resolution at 1.575 GB each and 4 low-resolution at 0.148 GB each.

The loop is two-stage: 120 killMS calls and 19 DDFacet calls, at a default output of 20,000×20,000 pixels at 1.5 arcsec. On the profiling machine — an HPE ProLiant DL385 Gen10 Plus with two AMD EPYC 7543 32-core processors and 512 GB of RAM, half of it configured as shared memory — a single node takes 68.87 hours. That time splits 53.40 % to killMS, 33.87 % to DDFacet, and the remaining 12.09 % across steps the profiler did not label — most likely DDFacet or killMS sub-stages rather than idle time.

The measured parallel run

The parallel version ran on the Jean Zay cpu partition — 24 nodes, 960 CPUs — over an 8-hour integration LOFAR dataset, as reported in the SC26 paper. It finished in 8.7 hours, about 7.9× faster than the 68.8-hour single node, at 31 % mean CPU usage and 24.3 % memory usage.

Eight hours of observation processed in 8.7 hours is close to a 1:1 ratio between telescope time and processing time. That ratio matters for the SKA: as the volumes grow, processing has to keep pace with observation, and storage itself becomes a budget.

The scaling, from one node to twenty-four:

  1. 1 node — 68.8 hours.
  2. 24 nodes — 8.7 hours, at 31 % mean CPU and 24.3 % memory.
  3. Speedup — ≈ 7.9×.

Hardening toward production

To make the DDF Pipeline ready for production processing of SKA data, effort has gone into documentation, multi-node robustness fixes, unit tests, and integration testing on the French supercomputers.
